subjects.name: Leonardo da Vinci
clues: Born in 1452 near a small Tuscan town, he was the son of a local notary.
He trained in the Florence workshop of the artist Andrea del Verrocchio.
He filled notebooks with designs for flying machines, written in mirror script.
He painted a famous Last Supper on a monastery dining-hall wall in Milan.
The Renaissance genius who painted the Mona Lisa.
subjects.fact: He spent his final years in France as a guest of King Francis I.

subjects.name: Michelangelo
clues: Born in 1475 in Caprese, he was nursed as a baby by a stonecutter's wife.
He saw himself as a sculptor first and took on big painting jobs unwillingly.
In his early twenties he carved the Pieta now in St. Peter's Basilica.
In old age he designed the great dome of St. Peter's Basilica in Rome.
The Renaissance master who carved David and painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling.

subjects.name: Vincent van Gogh
clues: Born in 1853, he worked as an art dealer and a preacher before he took up painting.
He made about 2,000 artworks in little more than a decade.
He sold very few paintings in his lifetime and relied on his brother Theo.
In Arles, in southern France, he painted bright vases of sunflowers.
The Dutch post-impressionist who painted The Starry Night.

subjects.name: Pablo Picasso
clues: Born in Malaga in 1881, he could draw like a trained artist as a young boy.
His early 'Blue Period' paintings were made almost entirely in shades of blue.
He spent most of his adult life in France and made tens of thousands of artworks.
Together with Georges Braque, he invented the style called Cubism.
The Spanish artist who painted the anti-war masterpiece Guernica.

subjects.name: Claude Monet
clues: Born in Paris in 1840, he grew up in the port of Le Havre on the Normandy coast.
His 1872 painting of a harbour at sunrise gave a whole art movement its name.
He painted the same haystacks and cathedral again and again in changing light.
He built a garden with a Japanese-style footbridge at his home in Giverny.
The Impressionist master famous for his paintings of water lilies.

subjects.name: Frida Kahlo
clues: Born in 1907 in Coyoacan, in a house now known as the Blue House.
After a terrible bus accident at 18, she began painting while recovering in bed.
About a third of all her paintings are self-portraits.
She was married to the famous muralist Diego Rivera.
The Mexican painter of bold self-portraits with flowers in her hair and a unibrow.

subjects.name: Rembrandt
clues: Born in Leiden in 1606, he moved to Amsterdam to work as a portrait painter.
He painted, drew and etched dozens of self-portraits across his life.
He was a master of light and shadow in the Dutch Golden Age.
His huge group portrait of a city militia company is known as The Night Watch.
The Dutch master whose Night Watch is the star of Amsterdam's Rijksmuseum.

subjects.name: Salvador Dalí
clues: Born in 1904 in Figueres, a town in Catalonia.
He designed the daisy-shaped logo of the Chupa Chups lollipop brand.
He worked with Walt Disney on a short film, Destino, finished decades later.
He was famous for his long, waxed, upturned moustache.
The Spanish Surrealist who painted melting clocks in The Persistence of Memory.

subjects.name: Mona Lisa
clues: This small portrait was begun in Florence around 1503 and worked on for years.
Its sitter is thought to be the wife of a Florentine silk merchant.
It was stolen in 1911 by a handyman and recovered two years later.
It hangs behind bulletproof glass in the Louvre in Paris.
Leonardo da Vinci's portrait of a woman with a famously mysterious smile.
subjects.fact: It is painted on a wooden poplar panel, not on canvas.

subjects.name: The Starry Night
clues: Painted in June 1889, it shows the view from an asylum window in southern France.
A tall, dark, flame-like cypress tree rises in its foreground.
It has hung in the Museum of Modern Art in New York since 1941.
Its sky is full of swirling blue and yellow whirls above a sleeping village.
Vincent van Gogh's most famous view of a swirling night sky.

subjects.name: The Last Supper
clues: This mural was painted in the 1490s on a monastery dining-hall wall in Milan.
Its painter tried an experimental method on dry plaster, so it soon began to flake.
A doorway was later cut through the bottom of the scene.
It shows the moment Jesus says one of his twelve disciples will betray him.
Leonardo da Vinci's famous painting of Jesus's final meal with his apostles.

subjects.name: The Scream
clues: First made in 1893, it exists in several versions in paint, pastel and print.
Its artist said it came from a walk when the sunset turned the sky blood red.
Versions of it were stolen from museums in Oslo in 1994 and 2004, then recovered.
Its wavy orange sky hangs over a fjord, seen from a bridge.
Edvard Munch's picture of a figure clutching its face in horror.

subjects.name: Girl with a Pearl Earring
clues: Painted around 1665, it is a study of a face rather than a portrait of a known person.
Its young subject wears a blue and yellow turban.
It hangs in the Mauritshuis museum in The Hague.
A 1999 novel and a 2003 film with Scarlett Johansson imagined the story behind it.
Johannes Vermeer's painting of a young woman with a large shining jewel at her ear.
subjects.fact: It is sometimes called the 'Mona Lisa of the North'.

subjects.name: The Persistence of Memory
clues: Painted in 1931, this small canvas measures only about 24 by 33 centimetres.
Its background shows the rocky coast of Catalonia.
It has belonged to New York's Museum of Modern Art since 1934.
A strange pale creature lies asleep on the ground in its middle.
Salvador Dali's Surrealist painting of soft, melting pocket watches.

subjects.name: Guernica
clues: Painted in 1937 for the Spanish pavilion at the Paris World's Fair.
It is painted only in black, white and shades of grey.
It shows the bombing of a Basque town during the Spanish Civil War.
It was kept in New York until Spain became a democracy, returning in 1981.
Pablo Picasso's huge anti-war painting, now in Madrid.

subjects.name: The Creation of Adam
clues: Painted around 1511, it is one of nine scenes from the Book of Genesis on a famous ceiling.
Its artist painted it in fresco while standing on tall scaffolding.
Some doctors have argued that the shape around God looks like a human brain.
God reaches out to give life to the very first man.
Michelangelo's Sistine Chapel scene of two nearly touching fingers.

subjects.name: David
clues: Finished in 1504, it was carved from a block of marble other sculptors had given up on.
This marble figure stands about 5.17 metres tall.
It first stood outside the town hall of Florence, where a copy stands today.
It shows a young biblical hero before his fight with Goliath.
Michelangelo's famous marble statue of the giant-slaying shepherd boy.

subjects.name: The Thinker
clues: It was first made as part of a huge bronze doorway called The Gates of Hell.
It was first meant to show the poet Dante, gazing down at his Inferno.
Many full-size bronze casts of it stand in cities around the world.
A famous cast sits in the garden of the Rodin Museum in Paris.
Auguste Rodin's bronze of a seated man resting his chin on his hand.

subjects.name: Venus de Milo
clues: Carved around 150 to 125 BCE, it was dug up by a farmer on a Greek island in 1820.
It is made of marble and stands just over two metres tall.
It is thought to show Aphrodite, the Greek goddess of love and beauty.
Its arms were lost long ago and have never been found.
The famous armless marble goddess displayed at the Louvre in Paris.

subjects.name: Pietà
clues: Carved in 1498 and 1499, when its sculptor was only in his early twenties.
It is the only work its sculptor ever signed, on a sash across Mary's chest.
It was damaged by a man with a hammer in 1972 and carefully restored.
It shows the Virgin Mary holding the body of Jesus across her lap.
Michelangelo's marble masterpiece, behind glass in St. Peter's Basilica.

subjects.name: William Shakespeare
clues: Baptised in 1564, he grew up in a market town on the River Avon.
He was an actor and part-owner of a successful London theatre company.
His company performed at the round Globe Theatre beside the Thames.
He is credited with inventing or popularising hundreds of English words.
The playwright of Romeo and Juliet, Hamlet and Macbeth.

subjects.name: Jane Austen
clues: Born in 1775 in a Hampshire village, the daughter of a clergyman.
Her novels were published without her name; one was signed simply 'By a Lady'.
She spent her final years in the village of Chawton and died in Winchester.
Her portrait appears on the Bank of England 10-pound note first issued in 2017.
The English novelist of Pride and Prejudice and Emma.

subjects.name: Charles Dickens
clues: Born in Portsmouth in 1812, he was sent to work in a shoe-polish factory at 12.
Most of his novels first came out in monthly or weekly instalments.
His books exposed the poverty and child labour of Victorian England.
He gave hugely popular public readings of his work in Britain and America.
The author who created Ebenezer Scrooge, Oliver Twist and David Copperfield.

subjects.name: Mark Twain
clues: Born in Missouri in 1835 when Halley's Comet was visible, he died at its return in 1910.
Before he became a writer he worked as a riverboat pilot on the Mississippi.
His pen name was a riverboat call meaning the water was two fathoms deep.
His boyhood home of Hannibal inspired the setting of his most famous novels.
The American author of The Adventures of Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn.

subjects.name: J. K. Rowling
clues: Born in 1965 near Bristol, she later taught English as a foreign language in Portugal.
She wrote much of her first novel in cafes in Edinburgh.
Her first book was turned down by many publishers before one said yes.
Her publisher asked for initials, fearing boys might not read a book by a woman.
The author of the Harry Potter books.

subjects.name: Agatha Christie
clues: Born in Torquay, Devon, in 1890, she worked in a hospital pharmacy during the First World War.
Her knowledge of poisons from that job appears in many of her mysteries.
In 1926 she vanished for eleven days, sparking a huge national search.
Her play The Mousetrap opened in London in 1952 and was still running 70 years later.
The 'Queen of Crime' who created Hercule Poirot and Miss Marple.

subjects.name: Leo Tolstoy
clues: Born in 1828 into a noble family on a country estate south of Moscow.
As a young army officer he wrote about the siege of Sevastopol in the Crimean War.
In later life he embraced simple living and non-violence, inspiring Gandhi.
His novel Anna Karenina opens with a famous line about happy families.
The Russian author of the giant novel War and Peace.

subjects.name: Homer
clues: This ancient poet is traditionally said to have been blind.
Several ancient Greek cities claimed to be his birthplace.
Some scholars doubt that he was a single real person at all.
The epics credited to him were sung aloud long before they were written down.
The Greek poet credited with the Iliad and the Odyssey.

subjects.name: Gabriel García Márquez
clues: Born in Aracataca, Colombia, in 1927, he was largely raised by his grandparents.
He began his working life as a newspaper journalist.
He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1982.
He is the best-known writer of the style called magical realism.
The Colombian author of One Hundred Years of Solitude.

subjects.name: J. R. R. Tolkien
clues: Born in 1892 in Bloemfontein, South Africa, he moved to England as a small child.
He fought in the Battle of the Somme during the First World War.
He was a professor of Old English at the University of Oxford.
He invented whole languages, including the Elvish tongues of Middle-earth.
The author of The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings.

subjects.name: Don Quixote
clues: Published in two parts, in 1605 and 1615, it is often called the first modern novel.
Its author, Miguel de Cervantes, lost the use of his left hand in a sea battle.
Its hero is a country gentleman who reads so many romances he sets out as a knight.
He rides a bony old horse, Rocinante, with his loyal squire Sancho Panza.
The Spanish novel whose hero charges at windmills, believing they are giants.

subjects.name: Pride and Prejudice
clues: Published in 1813, it was first drafted under the title First Impressions.
It follows the five Bennet sisters and their mother's hunt for good marriages.
Its witty heroine Elizabeth at first dislikes the proud, wealthy Mr Darcy.
Its first line says a rich single man must be in want of a wife.
Jane Austen's most famous novel, the love story of Elizabeth Bennet and Mr Darcy.

subjects.name: Frankenstein
clues: First published without its author's name in 1818, when she was just 20.
It began as an entry in a ghost-story contest at a villa near Lake Geneva.
Its subtitle compares its hero to the Titan who stole fire: The Modern Prometheus.
In it, a young scientist builds a living creature and then abandons it.
Mary Shelley's gothic novel about a scientist and the monster he makes.
subjects.fact: In the novel the creature is never given a name.

subjects.name: Moby-Dick
clues: Published in 1851, it sold poorly and was largely forgotten until the 1920s.
Its author had sailed on a whaling ship himself as a young man.
Its narrator begins by asking readers to call him Ishmael.
Captain Ahab hunts the great white whale that took his leg.
Herman Melville's novel about the hunt for a white whale.

subjects.name: Nineteen Eighty-Four
clues: Published in 1949, it imagines a future Britain ruled by an all-seeing Party.
Its hero, Winston Smith, secretly keeps a forbidden diary.
Its rulers invent Newspeak, a language designed to limit what people can think.
Its dreaded Room 101 holds each prisoner's worst fear.
George Orwell's novel whose posters warn 'Big Brother is watching you'.

subjects.name: One Hundred Years of Solitude
clues: First published in Buenos Aires in 1967, it became a worldwide bestseller.
Its story follows seven generations of the Buendia family.
It is set in Macondo, a made-up town in Colombia.
It is the most famous example of the style called magical realism.
Gabriel Garcia Marquez's masterpiece, which opens with a colonel facing a firing squad.

subjects.name: The Hobbit
clues: First published in 1937, it grew out of stories its author told his children.
Its author drew its maps and illustrations himself.
Its hero joins thirteen dwarves on a quest to win back treasure from a dragon.
On the journey its hero finds a magic ring in a dark mountain cave.
J. R. R. Tolkien's tale of Bilbo Baggins and the dragon Smaug.

subjects.name: Sherlock Holmes
clues: He first appeared in 1887 in the story A Study in Scarlet.
He plays the violin and solves cases through brilliant deduction.
His loyal friend and storyteller is Dr John Watson.
He lives at 221B Baker Street in London.
Arthur Conan Doyle's great detective in a deerstalker hat.

subjects.name: Harry Potter
clues: He first appeared in a children's novel published in 1997.
He grew up in a cupboard under the stairs at his aunt and uncle's house.
He has a lightning-bolt scar on his forehead.
His best friends are Ron Weasley and Hermione Granger.
The boy wizard of Hogwarts created by J. K. Rowling.

subjects.name: Hercule Poirot
clues: He first appeared in 1920 in The Mysterious Affair at Styles.
He is a retired police officer from Belgium who settles in England.
He is proud of his neat moustache and his 'little grey cells'.
He solved the Murder on the Orient Express and Death on the Nile.
Agatha Christie's famous Belgian detective.

subjects.name: Count Dracula
clues: He first appeared in an 1897 novel told through letters and diary entries.
He was created by the Irish writer Bram Stoker.
He sleeps in a coffin and can turn into a bat.
He lives in a castle in the Carpathian Mountains of Transylvania.
The most famous vampire in all of literature.

subjects.name: Robinson Crusoe
clues: He first appeared in a 1719 novel presented as a real-life memoir.
His tale is often linked to a real Scottish sailor marooned on a Pacific island.
He spends 28 years on a remote island after a shipwreck.
He names his companion Friday after the day they first meet.
Daniel Defoe's famous shipwrecked castaway.

subjects.name: Tom Sawyer
clues: He first appeared in an 1876 novel set in a town on the Mississippi River.
He lives with his Aunt Polly and his half-brother Sid.
He tricks other boys into paying him for the chance to whitewash a fence.
His best friend is Huckleberry Finn.
Mark Twain's mischievous boy hero from St. Petersburg, Missouri.

subjects.name: Frodo Baggins
clues: He first appeared in 1954 in the opening volume of a famous fantasy story.
He lives at Bag End in the Shire.
He inherits a dangerous ring from his elderly relative Bilbo.
His loyal gardener and friend is Samwise Gamgee.
The hobbit who carries the One Ring to Mount Doom.

subjects.name: Peter Pan
clues: He first appeared in a 1902 novel for adults, then in a 1904 stage play.
He lives in Neverland with the Lost Boys.
His enemy is Captain Hook, who lost a hand to a crocodile.
His fairy companion is Tinker Bell.
The flying boy who never grows up, created by J. M. Barrie.

subjects.name: Zeus
clues: His sacred symbols include the eagle, the oak tree and the thunderbolt.
As a baby he was hidden on Crete so his father could not swallow him.
He overthrew his father Cronus and the Titans.
The Romans knew him as Jupiter.
The king of the Greek gods, who rules from Mount Olympus.

subjects.name: Thor
clues: His chariot is pulled across the sky by two goats.
A day of the English week is named after him.
His father is Odin, the chief of the gods.
His hammer, Mjolnir, always returns to his hand.
The red-bearded Norse god of thunder.

subjects.name: King Arthur
clues: Early Welsh poems and a 12th-century history of British kings tell his story.
His wise wizard adviser is Merlin.
His queen is Guinevere and his greatest knight is Lancelot.
He gathers his knights around a Round Table at Camelot.
The legendary British ruler who pulled the sword from the stone.

subjects.name: Hercules
clues: As a baby he strangled two snakes that were sent to his cradle to kill him.
He was the son of Zeus and a mortal woman, Alcmene.
He had to complete twelve famous labours as a punishment.
One of his tasks was to kill the Nemean lion and wear its skin.
The Greek hero of legendary strength, best known today by his Roman name.

subjects.name: Medusa
clues: She was one of three sisters known as the Gorgons.
The winged horse Pegasus sprang from her blood.
The hero Perseus used a polished shield so he never looked at her directly.
Anyone who looked straight at her face was turned to stone.
The Greek monster with living snakes instead of hair.

subjects.name: Anubis
clues: He was usually shown as a man with the head of a black wild dog.
He watched over embalming and the making of mummies.
At the weighing of the heart, a dead person's heart was balanced against a feather.
He guided the souls of the dead through the underworld.
The jackal-headed Egyptian god of the dead.

subjects.name: Achilles
clues: His mother, the sea nymph Thetis, dipped him in a magical river as a baby.
He was the greatest Greek warrior at the siege of Troy.
He killed the Trojan prince Hector to avenge his friend Patroclus.
He was finally killed by an arrow shot by the Trojan prince Paris.
The hero whose only weak spot was his heel.
